transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-17
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lena (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood CSM); Maya (Acero SRE), Jonah (Acero CTO), Priya (Platform), Ravi (Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Discussed recent availability degradation after model rollout, identified cascading fallback misrouting and prefix cache invalidation as likely contributors. Agreed to share traces, run benches, and tighten canary/fallback policy. Action items assigned.

Topics: incident timeline; root causes brainstorm (routing, KV cash, canary sizes); security/audit asks; next steps for runbooks and benching

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Okay, thanks everyone for joining, we'll give folks a few seconds to pop in, um, quick agenda — surface the root cause for the 9-12 degradation, go over the mitigation steps we recommended, and align on action items and follow-ups.
[00:18] Maya: Hey Samir, thanks. For context we had a model rollout on Friday, and after about three hours we started to see increased 5xx and tail latency. A lot of the traffic was going to our canary but then during the scaling up we saw timeouts.
[00:34] Jonah: Yeah, to add, the backend microservice that does postprocessing also started to queue which amplified the problem, it wasn't only the model, there was this circuit where requests would backlog and then we hit a throttle.
[00:49] Lena: Right, and the logs we got from you look like there were a few long running KV cache invalidations — apologies, K-V cash — that ended up causing retries and replays which increased request amplification.
[01:06] Priya: We did change the prefix routing in our edge last week to route any unknown model-id to a fallback route, that may have been a contributing factor. We tried to be safe but we might have over-broaded it.
[01:22] Diego: Quick clarifying question — when you say fallback route, is that a lower-capacity model or an internal stub?
[01:29] Maya: It's a smaller model hosted in our Dedicated pool, so yes lower capacity but still counted as a full request, and when many requests fell back it overloaded some pools.
[01:38] Samir: Okay that's helpful. Two things we want to unpack: routing policy granularity and how the KV cache TTLs and invalidation are configured. On the Redis side, are you using a shared cluster across services?
[01:51] Maya: Yep shared Redis cluster, separate namespaces per service, but same node set. We saw a spike in eviction which coincided with the first error cascade.
[02:01] Lena: That eviction timing could produce a burst of cold KV loads into the model runtime, causing the runtime to block on cache warmup — that plus retries will shoot up p95.
[02:14] Jonah: We also noticed traces showing a handful of requests with two to three sequential retries within 200ms windows, I think the client side retry policy might be too aggressive.
[02:24] Priya: Our client policy is exponential backoff but with low jitter, we tuned it to be faster for UX.
[02:31] Samir: That low jitter is risky in high contention situations. For an LLM environment we normally advise adding more jitter plus bounded retries and ensuring the fallback route has rate limits so it doesn't become a sinkhole.
[02:45] Ravi: From a security and audit perspective, we need to ensure we can show the sequence of events — who triggered the rollout, timestamps, and audit logs. We also have to confirm retention windows for the request traces.
[02:58] Diego: Redwood has audit logging options — Samir, maybe you can point to the right doc for what we can share?
[03:05] Samir: Sure, I'll post the Redwood audit-log export guide, and we can map fields to your compliance needs. I also want to mention a pattern we recommend: do canaries that live for shorter windows and use traffic shapers to slowly step up — that avoids the sudden shock.
[03:20] Maya: One more operational note — during the event our autoscaler backed off because it saw a lot of short-lived failures. The scaling policy was too conservative for that kind of request profile.
[03:32] Lena: Autoscaler tuning matters; in the short term, increasing the target cpu threshold and enabling burst capacity might help. Longer term we want better tail latency visibility so we can see the p99 before we hit a cascade.
[03:47] Jonah: Can you outline a step-by-step for the safe rollback path? We want playbooks so our on-call doesn't improvise.
[03:55] Samir: Sure, rough rollback playbook: 1) pause new rollouts, 2) route new traffic to pre-defined stable model-id, 3) pin model variant, 4) warm KV cache with priming traffic, 5) monitor p95/p99 for 10 minutes before resuming. We'll send a template.
[04:15] Priya: For priming traffic, do you suggest synthetic or real traffic?
[04:20] Lena: Synthetic is ok for key prefixes but real traffic for long-tail prompts is best; mix both and limit overall QPS while priming.
[04:28] Maya: We have a feature flag system that can do a 0.5% shadow traffic — we can use that to prime without exposing to customers.
[04:36] Samir: Great. On the security front Ravi, do you have any redlines for sharing traces to Redwood?
[04:42] Ravi: We can share filtered traces, PII removed, but need to keep an audit trail and a retention note. Also we need to know how Redwood stores those logs if you ingest them.
[04:53] Samir: We use encrypted buckets in our private tenant for customers who share logs; that can be scoped with an expiration and access controls — I'll include the storage details in the doc.
[05:02] Diego: One other item — you mentioned the fallback route overwhelmed Dedicated pools. Have you considered throttling fallback traffic or using a queueing buffer?
[05:12] Lena: Yes, rate limiting fallback combined with token-bucket smoothing prevents sudden spikes. Also consider routing fallback to a smaller model with a much lower concurrency cap so it fails fast rather than queue.
[05:25] Jonah: But failing fast impacts UX; some product folks will push back. We need to balance SLA vs user-facing errors.
[05:33] Priya: For us the priority is to protect core revenue flows, not peripheral prompts, so we can set route-level priorities.
[05:40] Samir: That aligns — implement routing priorities and make the fallback degrade graceful by returning a cached result or a short explanation to the user.
[05:48] Maya: Can you also recommend specific KV cache TTL settings? We ran with 300s by default.
[05:54] Lena: 300s is fine for many keys but for prefix-level cache it's often better to have a staged TTL: short-lived ephemeral keys (30-60s) and longer TTLs for model metadata. Also ensure your warmup path primes the hot keys pre-rollout.
[06:10] Jonah: We have a question about private vs hosted — our security team wants private due to logs, but Dedicated in the hosted environment was cheaper. Thoughts?
[06:19] Samir: Private gives you the strongest control and local KMS integration; Dedicated (hosted) gives good isolation but less control over network. We can run the same runtime in both modes; it's mostly about how much control you need over audit and key management.
[06:33] Ravi: If we go Private we need HSM/KMS integration and formal attestations. Can Redwood provide an architecture diagram for that?
[06:40] Samir: Yes, we'll share an architecture diagram and the list of supported KMS/HSM partners.
[06:44] [10:00 later — mid-call jump to technical deep dive section]
[10:00] Lena: Okay diving into traces — I see repeated 502s originating from the postprocess service, followed by a waterfall of retries. That service had an unbounded work queue which is something to fix asap.
[10:17] Maya: Right, we opened a ticket to cap the queue and to add backpressure signals to the upstream gateway.
[10:24] Lena: Good. Also, on the Redwood side, there's a knob in our runtime to limit KV concurrency per request worker which prevents head-of-line blocking. We'll show you the config param in the follow-up doc.
[10:36] Samir: For benching, Lena will run a test case that simulates 1k QPS with 10% long-tail prompts and measure p50/p95/p99 across Hosted vs Dedicated with the same model. We'll include priming steps and seed keys.
[10:53] Priya: Make sure the bench uses our real prompt distribution, not synthetic short prompts.
[10:58] Lena: Agreed, we'll accept a sample of your prompt corpus and generate requests that mimic the distribution.
[11:06] Jonah: On the playbook front we want a one-sheet for on-call — what are the top 6 things to do in the first 10 minutes?
[11:12] Diego: We'll draft that: pause rollouts, reduce canary traffic to zero, check cache eviction metrics, review audit events, roll back model if necessary, notify product.
[11:22] Maya: One nuance — pause rollouts is easy but sometimes pipelines auto-resume; we need orchestration guardrails to prevent auto-resume.
[11:30] Samir: We can add a checklist item to disable auto-advance or require manual resume in your CD system.
[11:37] Priya: For remediation steps we also want to test a synthetic priming run before re-enabling; do you provide a priming tool or script?
[11:44] Lena: We have a sample priming script in the repo and we'll tailor it to your keys.
[11:48] Jonah: Are there any configuration defaults you recommend to avoid this class of incidents?
[11:53] Samir: Defaults: conservative client-side retries (3 max, jittered), rate-limited fallback routes, KV concurrency limit 8 per worker, canary window 15-30 minutes with step increases at 2x intervals, and autoscaler min replicas > 2 for model pools.
[12:10] Ravi: Also include how long you retain request-level diagnostics — our auditors want 90 days for certain flows.
[12:18] Samir: We'll document retention and how to export a subset for compliance.
[12:24] Priya: One last question — in the immediate term to stop the bleeding what should we do? We're mid-week and product folks want a fast fix.
[12:31] Samir: Short-term: stop rollouts, reduce fallback QPS, add rate limits on the fallback route to 10% of normal capacity, disable aggressive client retries, and run a cache warmup script. We'll send step-by-step.
[12:46] Maya: We'll do that and upload traces. Also we'll enable the queue cap on postprocess.
[12:52] Samir: Great. Let's recap action items and confirm follow-up meeting.
[13:00] Diego: Recap: Samir to send canary/fallback docs and architecture for private deployment; Lena to run Dedicated vs Hosted bench; Maya to share traces; Ravi to finalize audit requirements; follow-up deep dive on 2025-09-24.
[13:18] Jonah: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[13:22] Samir: Thanks, we'll put the notes and links into the CRM and follow-up in email.

End of transcript.
